cases.abstract: FlashAttention-2 addresses costs that remain after attention's quadratic intermediate matrices have been removed from high-bandwidth GPU memory. Tiled exact attention can still underuse the hardware because normalization is expensive relative to matrix multiplication, too few thread blocks are available, or warps must exchange partial outputs. The method postpones output normalization, distributes work across sequence blocks as well as batches and heads, and assigns query rows to different warps so that forward outputs do not require a cross-warp reduction. It preserves the attention computation without approximation and uses auxiliary memory linear in sequence length. Across the tested A100 attention configurations, FlashAttention-2 is 1.7-3.0 times faster than FlashAttention and 3-10 times faster than standard PyTorch attention. On eight A100 GPUs, training 1.3B- and 2.7B-parameter GPT-style models benefits more at 8k than at 2k contexts, with throughput reaching 225 TFLOPs/s per GPU. For multi-query decoding, a separate partitioning strategy spreads KV-cache loading across thread blocks and achieves attention-kernel speedups of up to seven times over FasterTransformer. These results show how matching work distribution to the workload bottleneck improves performance beyond eliminating intermediate storage.
cases.methods: The forward pass of FlashAttention-2 accumulates attention for one query block without repeatedly normalizing its partial output. For each key/value block, it maintains a running row maximum, a sum of exponentials measured relative to that maximum, and an unnormalized value-weighted accumulator. If the maximum changes, both existing sums are multiplied by the exponential of the old maximum minus the new one before the new block is added. Only after all blocks have been processed is the accumulator divided by the final exponential sum. This produces the full softmax-weighted output while replacing repeated normalization with a single final operation, reducing work that cannot use the GPU's fast matrix-multiplication units. Saving each row's logsumexp then allows probabilities to be recomputed during backpropagation instead of stored as a quadratic matrix. The algorithm retains quadratic arithmetic in sequence length but requires only linear auxiliary memory.
cases.results: Longer contexts yield larger end-to-end gains over FlashAttention in the reported GPT-style training runs. On eight A100 80GB SXM4 GPUs, replacing FlashAttention with FlashAttention-2 raises throughput for the 1.3B-parameter model from 189 to 196 TFLOPs/s per GPU at a 2k context, but from 170 to 220 at 8k. The 2.7B-parameter model reaches 225 TFLOPs/s at 8k, compared with 175 for FlashAttention. This pattern indicates that faster attention kernels have a greater effect on overall throughput when attention accounts for more computation. The reported peak and its 72% model FLOPs utilization use a convention that counts the full causal attention matrix, unlike the mask-adjusted arithmetic used in kernel benchmarks. These rates therefore require their accounting conventions to remain explicit. At 16k sequence length, standard PyTorch attention runs out of memory in the kernel tests, while FlashAttention-2 still runs, retaining the memory advantage of avoiding quadratic intermediate storage.
cases.notes: The body reports a 2.8-fold maximum training speedup over the baseline without FlashAttention, but Table 1 gives 220 versus 72 TFLOPs/s for the 1.3B model at 8k, implying approximately 3.06-fold. The passages use table entries and avoid this conflicting maximum. H100-specific instructions and automatic block-size tuning are proposed work, not evaluated improvements. The linear-memory claim concerns auxiliary attention storage; arithmetic remains quadratic.

cases.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates Transformer generation by replacing some serial target-model evaluations with concurrent verification of a cheaper model's guesses. A proposal model generates several tokens, and the target model evaluates their conditional distributions in parallel. A probability-ratio acceptance test retains compatible guesses; when a guess is rejected, sampling from the positive residual between the target and proposal distributions restores the missing target probability mass. This correction preserves the target's sampling distribution for any proposal model, without retraining the target. The analysis relates accepted block length to distributional overlap and balances it against proposal cost. Its walltime prediction assumes independent, identically distributed acceptance rates, sufficiently long generations, and enough compute capacity for concurrent target evaluations to take no longer than one ordinary evaluation. In batch-one experiments with T5-XXL on a single TPU-v4, the 77M-parameter T5-small proposal model accelerates English-German translation by 2.6 times under standard sampling and 3.4 times under greedy decoding. Summarization speedups are 2.3 and 3.1 times, respectively. Larger proposal models increase acceptance but produce smaller speedups, showing why acceptance alone does not determine the latency benefit.
cases.methods: Speculative decoding verifies each proposed token x with acceptance probability min(1, p(x)/q(x)), where p and q are conditional distributions after the chosen sampling transformation. Accepted proposals contribute probability mass min(p(x), q(x)); on rejection, sampling from the normalized positive part of p - q supplies the remaining target mass. At the first rejection, later guesses are discarded and this correction supplies the next token. If every guess passes, an additional token is drawn directly from the target. Thus each iteration emits between one and gamma + 1 tokens while preserving the target distribution. Under independent, identically distributed acceptance rates with mean alpha, the expected count is 1 + alpha + ... + alpha^gamma. For sufficiently long generations, dividing that count by 1 + gamma*c predicts the speedup, where c is relative proposal latency and concurrent target evaluations are assumed to cost no more than one ordinary evaluation.
cases.results: For English-German translation with T5-XXL, the smallest tested proposal model gives the strongest latency improvement despite the lowest acceptance rate. Under standard sampling on a single TPU-v4 at batch size one, T5-small accepts proposals at a mean rate of 0.62 and achieves a 2.6-fold speedup, whereas T5-large raises acceptance to 0.71 but achieves only 1.4-fold speedup. These configurations use seven and three guesses, respectively, so the comparison reflects the model-and-speculation tradeoff rather than an isolated effect of proposal size. Greedy decoding with T5-small reaches 3.4-fold speedup and 0.75 acceptance, showing that the sampling transformation also changes the useful overlap. Summarization gains are smaller: 2.3-fold for standard sampling and 3.1-fold for greedy decoding. The results therefore favor inexpensive, sufficiently compatible proposals over maximizing acceptance alone. They do not establish reduced arithmetic work: rejected guesses waste computation, and acceleration depends on spare capacity for concurrent target evaluations.
cases.notes: Measured walltime improvements are limited to T5; the GPT-like and LaMDA experiments measure acceptance only. The runtime formula assumes i.i.d. acceptance and target evaluations that can run concurrently without increasing walltime, not a universal speed guarantee. The output-distribution guarantee does not assert that a run reproduces the same sampled token sequence.
